screens.title: Introduction to Network Automation and Programmability
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this chapter you will learn why network automation and programmability have become essential in modern enterprise infrastructures. Manual, command-line driven workflows served networks for decades, but as device counts and service expectations grow, those approaches create risk: human error, slow delivery, and inconsistent configurations. Automation lets engineers express changes as code or high-level intent, apply those changes across many devices reliably, and verify outcomes quickly. You will see how paradigms such as software-defined networking provide centralized control, how intent-based networking lets you state desired outcomes instead of device-by-device commands, and how orchestration coordinates multi-step workflows. We also cover the practical building blocks: APIs exposed by devices, data models like YANG, and common protocols used to interact with network platforms. Finally, we work through realistic pitfalls: start small, use version control, secure A P I credentials, and test in labs with rollback plans. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to identify high-value automation candidates, explain the role of APIs and data models, and propose a safe first automation approach for a branch-onboarding scenario. Think about one repetitive task in your environment you would prioritize for automation and why.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you will develop four core abilities that let you plan and begin automation safely. First, you will explain the main drivers and benefits of network automation: increased deployment speed, lower operational cost, improved consistency, and stronger security through repeatable checks. A concrete example is provisioning VLANs and access ports across multiple switches in minutes rather than manually. Second, you will differentiate traditional CLI workflows from programmatic approaches using APIs and structured data. You will learn why parsing CLI text is fragile compared to consuming JSON or XML from an A P I. Third, you will identify SDN, intent-based networking, and orchestration as standard approaches. You will be able to say what each achieves: abstraction and central control, outcome-driven configuration, and multi-step workflow coordination. Fourth, you will understand the foundational role of APIs and data models like YANG in making network programmability reliable. Each objective is tied to practical tasks: choose high-impact automation candidates, plan an Ansible or Python approach, and protect automation with version control and testing. Which of these objectives will you practice first in your environment?

screens.title: Practice-focused Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: This second objectives slide puts the prior goals into a practical skill frame you can act on. You will learn to identify automation candidates — repetitive, low-risk, high-impact tasks — and to map them to a suitable automation approach such as a Python script, an Ansible playbook, or an orchestration workflow. For example, creating identical VLANs and access-port assignments across ten switches is a prime candidate: it is repetitive, parameterizable, and low-risk when templated. Finally, you will be able to propose simple orchestration sequences that coordinate device configuration with service validation steps, such as configuring VLANs, applying interface settings, and then validating connectivity. These practical objectives are the bridge from theory to a safe first automation project.

screens.title: Manual CLI vs Programmatic Management
screens.narratorSegment: Let's compare manual CLI workflows to programmatic approaches and reveal why many teams move to APIs and data models. Manual CLI is immediate and familiar: an engineer logs into a device and types commands to change configuration. This works well for one-off fixes, but it becomes fragile at scale. Small differences between devices, typographical errors, and inconsistent application of settings lead to outages and long troubleshooting cycles. Programmatic management uses APIs or structured automation tools to express configuration as code or templates. Instead of parsing free-form command output, programs consume structured data formats such as JSON or XML returned by device APIs. A concrete example: creating a VLAN on two core switches manually requires repeating the CLI sequence on each device; programmatically you define the VLAN once with parameters and push it to all targets, ensuring uniform names and IDs. A common misconception is that APIs replace the need for network knowledge; in fact, automation amplifies mistakes if the logic is wrong. The correct approach is to codify operational knowledge, validate it in a lab, use version control, and run staged deployments. Consider the question: which repetitive task would cause the biggest operational risk if performed manually today?

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › CLI vs API
Manual CLI
Definition
Human-driven configuration using device consoles or SSH sessions and typed commands.
Pain points
  • Prone to typing errors and inconsistencies between devices.
  • Hard to track changes without disciplined records.
  • Slow at scale for frequent operations.
When to use
One-off troubleshooting and exploratory tasks where speed of thinking matters most.
Programmatic Management
Definition
Use of APIs, data models, and code to apply and verify network state across many devices.
Advantages
  • Consistent application of templates and parameters.
  • Structured responses allow reliable parsing and validation.
  • Enables testing, versioning, and rollback.
Misconception
APIs don’t replace expertise: they require correct logic and validation to avoid scaling mistakes.

screens.title: Software-Defined Networking (SDN)
screens.narratorSegment: Software-Defined Networking is a paradigm that separates the control plane — the system that decides where traffic should go — from the data plane that forwards packets. This separation allows a centralized controller or a set of controllers to make routing and policy decisions for many devices, and to push consistent rules to the forwarding elements. An example: rather than configuring access control lists on dozens of switches individually, an SDN controller can install the required rules centrally and ensure they are applied uniformly. SDN principles are foundational to many automation strategies, even when a full SDN overlay is not deployed: centralized control and abstraction simplify consistent policy enforcement. A common misconception is that SDN removes all device-level configuration; in practice, SDN abstracts many details, but devices still require supporting software and interfaces. Key takeaway: SDN gives you the ability to program network behavior from a central point, enabling faster policy changes and easier verification. Ask yourself what policies in your network would benefit from central control. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) means centralized control reduces manual device-by-device configuration and makes policy changes and verification faster and more consistent.. In practical terms, decoupling control from forwarding for centralized policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › SDN
Software-Defined Networking
Core idea
Decouple control plane from data plane so centralized controllers can program forwarding behavior.
Concrete example
A controller pushes ACLs to multiple switches to enforce a security policy consistently across all sites.
Misconception
SDN doesn’t eliminate device configuration entirely; it abstracts and automates it from a central policy layer.
Why it matters
Faster, consistent policy changes; easier verification and rollback at scale.
Analogy
Think of SDN as a traffic manager that tells many traffic lights when to change, instead of adjusting each light individually.
Key Takeaway
Centralized decisions make coordinated changes safer and faster.

screens.title: Intent-Based Networking (IBN)
screens.narratorSegment: Intent-Based Networking changes the way we tell the network what to do. Instead of describing device-level commands, you express the desired outcome — the intent — in high-level terms, and the system translates that intent into device configurations and continuously monitors the network to ensure compliance. For example, rather than configuring NAT, access lists, and routes on each device, you declare that the branch network should reach a central service and meet a performance SLA. The IBN system then computes the necessary device changes and enforces them. This reduces human error because operators focus on business outcomes, not device syntax. A common misconception is thinking intent alone is sufficient; intent systems still require correct models, good telemetry, and robust translation engines. The practical implication is that your team must define clear intents and validation rules, and maintain them under version control just like code. A useful question to close with is: what outcome would you trust an intent system to enforce in your network today? Intent-Based Networking (IBN) means express desired outcomes, not commands; rely on translation and continuous validation to maintain that outcome.. In practical terms, from device commands to desired outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Intent-Based Networking
Intent-Based Networking
What it is
Declare the desired state of the network and let the system translate and enforce that state across devices.
Concrete example
Declare that branch traffic must reach central services with a latency SLA. The system applies routes, QoS, and verification checks to meet the intent.
Common pitfall
Relying on intent without telemetry or validation can hide mismatches between desired and actual state.
Why it matters
Focus on outcomes, reduce device-specific errors, and enable continuous compliance monitoring.
Check your understanding
Name one policy in your network that could be expressed as an intent and monitored automatically.

screens.title: Orchestration
screens.narratorSegment: Orchestration is the coordination of automated tasks that span multiple devices, domains, or tools. While an automation script may configure a single device, orchestration defines a sequence: provision VLANs on switches, configure router subinterfaces, deploy DHCP scope, and finally run connectivity checks. Orchestration systems handle dependencies, sequencing, retries, and error handling so complex changes execute reliably. For instance, onboarding a branch office is an orchestration problem: it requires ordered steps on core switches, access switches, routers, and verification tools. A misconception is to confuse orchestration with orchestration-only tools; effective orchestration often integrates scripting, configuration management, and APIs to execute each step. Orchestration also provides visibility into each task's success or failure, enabling selective rollbacks. The practical takeaway is to plan automation as workflows: identify the ordered steps, required inputs, validation points, and rollback actions. What sequence would you design for adding a new branch so that a failed step leaves the network in a safe state? Orchestration means treat multi-device changes as workflows with clear sequencing, validation, and rollback to ensure reliability.. In practical terms, coordinating multi-step workflows across systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › Orchestration
Orchestration: a workflow approach
1
Define steps
Example sequence for branch onboarding:
  1. Provision VLAN on core switches.
  2. Configure access ports on branch switches.
  3. Apply subinterface and DHCP on router.
  4. Run connectivity and policy checks.
Dependences
Ensure upstream devices are configured before downstream steps run.
Rollback
Design rollbacks so failed executions don’t leave partial, inconsistent state.
Visibility
Orchestration records each step and outcome to support retries and audits.
Analogy
Orchestration is like a conductor coordinating musicians so the whole piece runs in order and recovers from mistakes.

screens.title: APIs and Protocols: NETCONF & RESTCONF
screens.narratorSegment: Network devices expose programmatic interfaces so automation tools can interact reliably. Two commonly referenced protocols are NETCONF and RESTCONF. Both allow structured configuration and operational state retrieval from devices running modern network OSs such as IOS XE or NX-OS. NETCONF uses XML over a secure session and is often paired with YANG models. RESTCONF exposes similar capabilities over RESTful HTTP endpoints typically returning JSON or XML. A concrete scenario: a script retrieves interface state using RESTCONF, checks for discrepancies, and then calls NETCONF or RESTCONF to apply a corrected configuration. A common misconception is that RESTCONF always replaces NETCONF; in practice both coexist and tool choices depend on vendor support and data model availability. Practical guidance: prefer structured A P I access over parsing CLI output, authenticate A P I calls securely, and validate responses against expected models. Closing question: which A P I style does your current infrastructure support, and how would you test its responses in a lab? APIs and Protocols: NETCONF & RESTCONF means prefer structured apis like netconf and restconf over cli parsing, and validate responses against models.. In practical terms, how devices expose programmatic interfaces. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › APIs
NETCONF
Uses XML over secure sessions and works closely with YANG models to provide structured configuration and state operations.
RESTCONF
Provides a RESTful interface over HTTP to access configuration and operational data, often returning JSON or XML.
Practical tip
Authenticate API calls securely and test responses against expected data models in a lab before production.
Misconception
APIs eliminate need for network knowledge — they actually require accurate models and operator understanding to avoid automating errors.
Check
Verify the API endpoints on your devices in a lab by issuing read calls and confirming the returned JSON/XML matches expected YANG-derived structures.

screens.title: Data Models and YANG
screens.narratorSegment: Data models are the grammar that makes automation reliable. YANG is a widely used modeling language that describes configuration and operational state in a structured, vendor-agnostic way. When a device implements a YANG model, automation tools can request and set configuration as structured objects rather than parsing command-line text. For example, instead of scraping show interface output, an automation tool requests the interface structure in JSON using a model and can reliably extract IP addresses, status, and counters. This reduces brittleness when device software versions change the CLI output. A common misconception is that data models are only for large vendors; many modern network OSs provide YANG models. Practical advice: map your common configuration items to YANG model nodes and validate changes against the model before applying them. Closing question: which configuration elements in your environment would benefit most from being modeled and automated? Data Models and YANG means use yang and data models to exchange structured configuration and state, making automation predictable and durable.. In practical terms, structured, vendor-agnostic descriptions for configuration and state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 7 › Chapter 7.1 › YANG & Models
What is YANG?
A language to define the structure of configuration and operational data so tools can consume and validate it consistently.
Example
Request interface state as structured data and extract IP addresses and admin status without parsing CLI text.
Why it matters
Models make automation resilient to CLI changes and vendor differences by using a common structure.
Action
Inventory the configuration elements you automate and map them to YANG nodes to ensure predictable automation behavior.

screens.title: Mapping a Branch Onboarding to Automation
screens.narratorSegment: Now we apply the chapter material to a hands-on scenario: onboarding a new branch office. The task involves configuring a VLAN on two core switches, assigning access ports on an access switch, configuring a routed subinterface and DHCP on the router, and verifying connectivity to a central server. Begin by listing the CLI commands you would normally use for each device. Next, identify which parts are repetitive and parameterize them: VLAN ID, name, interface ranges, IP addresses, and DHCP pool names. For low-risk repeated steps like VLAN creation and access-port assignments, use an Ansible playbook with a Jinja2 template to keep configuration consistent. For the router subinterface and DHCP, a templated configuration applied via Ansible or a Python script with a structured payload is suitable. For verification, write a simple script that runs ping and parsing against the server IP and returns structured success/failure. Remember the implementation checklist: keep automation code in Git, secure credentials (don't store them in plain text), test in a lab, and prepare rollback commands. A final question to consider: which step would you automate first and how would you validate it in a safe environment?

screens.title: Common Pitfalls and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Implementing automation brings obvious benefits, but there are common mistakes teams make. The most frequent error is trying to automate everything at once without a clear, prioritized strategy. Start small: select repetitive, parameterizable tasks that reduce risk and provide measurable ROI. Another pitfall is poor management of automation code. Treat automation as software: use version control to track changes, perform code review, and enable rollbacks. Security mistakes are also common: never store A P I credentials in plaintext; use secure vaults and role-based access. Testing is essential — validate in a lab environment and include verification steps in your workflows. Finally, automation logic can amplify mistakes if it's incorrect; always include validation and staged rollouts. For example, deploy changes to a subset of devices and monitor for unintended consequences before full deployment. The practical checklist is: pick small candidates, use Git, secure credentials, write tests and verification, and prepare rollbacks. What governance steps will you apply to automation in your team? In practical terms, avoid automating everything at once; apply software practices to automation. fullNarratorScript:
Welcome. In this chapter you will learn why network automation and programmability have become essential in modern enterprise infrastructures. Manual, command-line driven workflows served networks for decades, but as device counts and service expectations grow, those approaches create risk: human error, slow delivery, and inconsistent configurations. Automation lets engineers express changes as code or high-level intent, apply those changes across many devices reliably, and verify outcomes quickly. You will see how paradigms such as software-defined networking provide centralized control, how intent-based networking lets you state desired outcomes instead of device-by-device commands, and how orchestration coordinates multi-step workflows. We also cover the practical building blocks: APIs exposed by devices, data models like YANG, and common protocols used to interact with network platforms. Finally, we work through realistic pitfalls: start small, use version control, secure A P I credentials, and test in labs with rollback plans. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to identify high-value automation candidates, explain the role of APIs and data models, and propose a safe first automation approach for a branch-onboarding scenario. Think about one repetitive task in your environment you would prioritize for automation and why.

In this chapter you will develop four core abilities that let you plan and begin automation safely. First, you will explain the main drivers and benefits of network automation: increased deployment speed, lower operational cost, improved consistency, and stronger security through repeatable checks. A concrete example is provisioning VLANs and access ports across multiple switches in minutes rather than manually. Second, you will differentiate traditional CLI workflows from programmatic approaches using APIs and structured data. You will learn why parsing CLI text is fragile compared to consuming JSON or XML from an A P I. Third, you will identify SDN, intent-based networking, and orchestration as standard approaches. You will be able to say what each achieves: abstraction and central control, outcome-driven configuration, and multi-step workflow coordination. Fourth, you will understand the foundational role of APIs and data models like YANG in making network programmability reliable. Each objective is tied to practical tasks: choose high-impact automation candidates, plan an Ansible or Python approach, and protect automation with version control and testing. Which of these objectives will you practice first in your environment?

This second objectives slide puts the prior goals into a practical skill frame you can act on. You will learn to identify automation candidates — repetitive, low-risk, high-impact tasks — and to map them to a suitable automation approach such as a Python script, an Ansible playbook, or an orchestration workflow. For example, creating identical VLANs and access-port assignments across ten switches is a prime candidate: it is repetitive, parameterizable, and low-risk when templated. You will also practice safe automation habits: keep automation code in version control so you can review and roll back changes, secure A P I credentials rather than embedding them in plain scripts, and test changes in a lab before production. Finally, you will be able to propose simple orchestration sequences that coordinate device configuration with service validation steps, such as configuring VLANs, applying interface settings, and then validating connectivity. These practical objectives are the bridge from theory to a safe first automation project.

Let's compare manual CLI workflows to programmatic approaches and reveal why many teams move to APIs and data models. Manual CLI is immediate and familiar: an engineer logs into a device and types commands to change configuration. This works well for one-off fixes, but it becomes fragile at scale. Small differences between devices, typographical errors, and inconsistent application of settings lead to outages and long troubleshooting cycles. Programmatic management uses APIs or structured automation tools to express configuration as code or templates. Instead of parsing free-form command output, programs consume structured data formats such as JSON or XML returned by device APIs. A concrete example: creating a VLAN on two core switches manually requires repeating the CLI sequence on each device; programmatically you define the VLAN once with parameters and push it to all targets, ensuring uniform names and IDs. A common misconception is that APIs replace the need for network knowledge; in fact, automation amplifies mistakes if the logic is wrong. The correct approach is to codify operational knowledge, validate it in a lab, use version control, and run staged deployments. Consider the question: which repetitive task would cause the biggest operational risk if performed manually today?

Software-Defined Networking is a paradigm that separates the control plane — the system that decides where traffic should go — from the data plane that forwards packets. This separation allows a centralized controller or a set of controllers to make routing and policy decisions for many devices, and to push consistent rules to the forwarding elements. An example: rather than configuring access control lists on dozens of switches individually, an SDN controller can install the required rules centrally and ensure they are applied uniformly. SDN principles are foundational to many automation strategies, even when a full SDN overlay is not deployed: centralized control and abstraction simplify consistent policy enforcement. A common misconception is that SDN removes all device-level configuration; in practice, SDN abstracts many details, but devices still require supporting software and interfaces. Key takeaway: SDN gives you the ability to program network behavior from a central point, enabling faster policy changes and easier verification. Ask yourself what policies in your network would benefit from central control. Software-Defined Networking (SDN) means centralized control reduces manual device-by-device configuration and makes policy changes and verification faster and more consistent.. In practical terms, decoupling control from forwarding for centralized policy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Intent-Based Networking changes the way we tell the network what to do. Instead of describing device-level commands, you express the desired outcome — the intent — in high-level terms, and the system translates that intent into device configurations and continuously monitors the network to ensure compliance. For example, rather than configuring NAT, access lists, and routes on each device, you declare that the branch network should reach a central service and meet a performance SLA. The IBN system then computes the necessary device changes and enforces them. This reduces human error because operators focus on business outcomes, not device syntax. A common misconception is thinking intent alone is sufficient; intent systems still require correct models, good telemetry, and robust translation engines. The practical implication is that your team must define clear intents and validation rules, and maintain them under version control just like code. A useful question to close with is: what outcome would you trust an intent system to enforce in your network today? Intent-Based Networking (IBN) means express desired outcomes, not commands; rely on translation and continuous validation to maintain that outcome.. In practical terms, from device commands to desired outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Orchestration is the coordination of automated tasks that span multiple devices, domains, or tools. While an automation script may configure a single device, orchestration defines a sequence: provision VLANs on switches, configure router subinterfaces, deploy DHCP scope, and finally run connectivity checks. Orchestration systems handle dependencies, sequencing, retries, and error handling so complex changes execute reliably. For instance, onboarding a branch office is an orchestration problem: it requires ordered steps on core switches, access switches, routers, and verification tools. A misconception is to confuse orchestration with orchestration-only tools; effective orchestration often integrates scripting, configuration management, and APIs to execute each step. Orchestration also provides visibility into each task's success or failure, enabling selective rollbacks. The practical takeaway is to plan automation as workflows: identify the ordered steps, required inputs, validation points, and rollback actions. What sequence would you design for adding a new branch so that a failed step leaves the network in a safe state? Orchestration means treat multi-device changes as workflows with clear sequencing, validation, and rollback to ensure reliability.. In practical terms, coordinating multi-step workflows across systems. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Network devices expose programmatic interfaces so automation tools can interact reliably. Two commonly referenced protocols are NETCONF and RESTCONF. Both allow structured configuration and operational state retrieval from devices running modern network OSs such as IOS XE or NX-OS. NETCONF uses XML over a secure session and is often paired with YANG models. RESTCONF exposes similar capabilities over RESTful HTTP endpoints typically returning JSON or XML. A concrete scenario: a script retrieves interface state using RESTCONF, checks for discrepancies, and then calls NETCONF or RESTCONF to apply a corrected configuration. A common misconception is that RESTCONF always replaces NETCONF; in practice both coexist and tool choices depend on vendor support and data model availability. Practical guidance: prefer structured A P I access over parsing CLI output, authenticate A P I calls securely, and validate responses against expected models. Closing question: which A P I style does your current infrastructure support, and how would you test its responses in a lab? This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Data models are the grammar that makes automation reliable. YANG is a widely used modeling language that describes configuration and operational state in a structured, vendor-agnostic way. When a device implements a YANG model, automation tools can request and set configuration as structured objects rather than parsing command-line text. For example, instead of scraping show interface output, an automation tool requests the interface structure in JSON using a model and can reliably extract IP addresses, status, and counters. This reduces brittleness when device software versions change the CLI output. A common misconception is that data models are only for large vendors; many modern network OSs provide YANG models. Practical advice: map your common configuration items to YANG model nodes and validate changes against the model before applying them. Closing question: which configuration elements in your environment would benefit most from being modeled and automated? Data Models and YANG means use yang and data models to exchange structured configuration and state, making automation predictable and durable.. In practical terms, structured, vendor-agnostic descriptions for configuration and state. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Now we apply the chapter material to a hands-on scenario: onboarding a new branch office. The task involves configuring a VLAN on two core switches, assigning access ports on an access switch, configuring a routed subinterface and DHCP on the router, and verifying connectivity to a central server. Next, identify which parts are repetitive and parameterize them: VLAN ID, name, interface ranges, IP addresses, and DHCP pool names. A final question to consider: which step would you automate first and how would you validate it in a safe environment?
